newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba repo add shows it wants no rate rise - dealers.
newsitem.headline: Buba repo add shows it wants no rate rise - dealers.

text.p: The Bundesbank's move to add a net 2.6 billion marks to the German money market on Wednesday is a sign that it does not want money market rates to rise for the time being, money market dealers said.
"The Bundesbank apparently does not want higher rates," one money market dealer said after the Bundesbank alloted 74.7 billion marks in its weekly repo allocation at a fixed rate of 3.00 percent.
"The Bundesbank appears to want to remain with fixed rate repos at 3.00 percent. But things may look different next week if the dollar rises above 1.90 marks."
A repo pact totalling 72.1 billion marks expired on Wednesday so the repo allocation meant that a net 2.6 billion marks flowed into the money market.
Dealers said money market rates were quoted in a range of 3.00 to 3.10 percent, little changed from 3.05/10 percent on Tuesday.

A heavy drain of funds from the money market might have been interpreted as a sign the Bundesbank was preparing the market for a return to variable-rate repo tenders and that it was encouraging banks to bid the key money market rate higher next week.
The mark's steep slide against the dollar has fuelled speculation that the Bundesbank may raise interest rates.

There has been speculation it may do so by switching from fixed-rate repo tenders -- at which it sets the rate itself -- to variable-rate tenders, at which the repo rate is determined by the rates at which banks bid for Bundesbank funds.

One dealer said the net addition of repo funds came as no surprise after a steep fall in commercial banks' deposits with the central bank on Tuesday -- a sign of liquidity shortage in the money market.
"It was obvious the Bundesbank had to add funds after the deposits figures fell, the dealer said."

Banks' deposits at the Bundesbank fell to 39.0 billion marks on Tuesday from 40.8 billion marks on Monday, while the average for the month through Tuesday was 40.7 billion marks, down from 41.1 billion marks on Monday.
The dealer predicted the Bundesbank would set to set further repo tenders at a fixed rate of 3.00 percent -- the rate that has prevailed since August 1996.
The Bundesbank's last central bank council meeting before its four-week summer break on July 24 took the unusual step of setting fixed-rate repo tenders for just two weeks.

The second of those repo pacts was allocated on Wednesday, leaving markets in the dark whether next week's repo tender will be a fixed-rate repo at 3.00 percent, a variable-rate repo, or a fixed-rate repo at a higher rate.
Theoretically, the Bundesbank does not have to say what form the tender will take until it invites bids from banks for repos next Tuesday.
But with markets speculating feverishly about whether the Bundesbank will shift to higher rates, the bank may make an announcement sooner, dealers said.

"I wouldn't be surprised if the Bundesbank waits until next Tuesday to announce what form the repo tender will take but it could be that the Bundesbank will make an announcement on Thursday to deflate market speculation," one dealer said.
But analysts doubt whether a return to variable rates repos with the likely effect of a slight rise in the repo rate to 3.10 percent or so would be enough to underpin the mark.
Some analysts even say the move might backfire and push the mark even lower.

In addition, with unemployment high, no sign of imminent inflation increases and consumer spending still largely stagnant, many analysts believe the Bundesbank has no need yet to usher in a cycle of interest rate increases.
--David Crossland, Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
